# Text has no natural axes {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The transform problem

To visualize language we must first make it **countable or geometric**:

| Transform | What becomes visible |
|---|---|
| Token counts | What's frequent |
| TF–IDF | What's *distinctive* |
| Topic models | What themes organize the corpus |
| Embeddings | What's *semantically near* what |

Each transform makes assumptions. The chart inherits all of them.

## Counting: from corpus to numbers

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
# One corpus for the whole deck: big enough for a readable word cloud, and made
# of real sentences so the concordance slide later has something to show.
docs = [
    "the model trains on data and the data shapes what the model can say",
    "data visualization turns numbers into pictures that people can read quickly",
    "a topic model finds themes hiding in a large corpus of text",
    "embeddings place similar text near similar text in a shared space",
    "people read pictures faster than they read tables of numbers",
    "text needs a transform before any visualization can begin at all",
    "a word cloud sizes each word by how often it appears in the text",
    "the sorted bar chart puts frequency on position and length",
    "stop words are removed because they appear in every document",
    "tf idf asks which words are frequent here and rare everywhere else",
    "a data scientist reads the chart and then reads the raw text",
    "machine learning models need clean data more than clever algorithms",
    "the corpus is small so every topic model result deserves suspicion",
    "good visualization design starts from the question not from the data",
    "social media text is noisy and full of repeated boilerplate phrases",
    "a language model can summarize text but it can also invent detail",
    "counting words is easy and interpreting the counts is the hard part",
    "data science borrows from statistics computing and visual design",
    "the same corpus gives different topics under different random seeds",
    "clean text first because preprocessing choices change every later chart",
    "a chart of word frequency hides the sentences the words came from",
    "readers trust a picture of data more than a table of the same data",
]
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
cv = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english")
counts = cv.fit_transform(docs)
freq = pd.Series(counts.sum(axis=0).A1, index=cv.get_feature_names_out()).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4))
freq.tail(10).plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#2E6E8E")
ax.set_title("A 22-document corpus → sorted term frequencies (stop words removed)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A **sorted bar chart** puts frequency on position and length, the two channels Week 2 ranked most accurate.

## Before you count: preprocessing is a transform {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer

ps = PorterStemmer()
stemmed_docs = [" ".join(ps.stem(w) for w in d.split()) for d in docs]

def top_terms(corpus, stop=None, n=8):
    v = CountVectorizer(stop_words=stop)
    m = v.fit_transform(corpus)
    s = pd.Series(m.sum(axis=0).A1, index=v.get_feature_names_out())
    return s.sort_values().tail(n), len(s)

panels = [("keep everything", *top_terms(docs, None)),
          ("drop stop words", *top_terms(docs, "english")),
          ("drop stop words,\nthen stem", *top_terms(stemmed_docs, "english"))]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.4, 2.4))
for ax, (name, s, vocab) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.barh(s.index, s.values, color="#2E6E8E")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\n({vocab} distinct terms)", fontsize=9)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The transform table starts at "token counts", but decisions have already been made by then.

- **Stop words.** Keep them and the chart is `the`, `and`, `of` — true and useless. Which list you drop is a choice: the standard English list removes `not`, which matters for anything about opinion.
- **Stemming.** `word` (3) and `words` (4) stay separate until you stem, then merge into **7** and overtake `model` — the ranking changed, not just the counts. Note the labels: Porter stemming chops suffixes, so `every` becomes `everi` and `visualization` collapses into `visual`. Lemmatisation is slower and returns real words.

None of this is visible in the finished chart, so name the preprocessing in the caption.

## One word or two? n-grams {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
def ngram_top(rng, n=8):
    v = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english", ngram_range=rng)
    m = v.fit_transform(docs)
    s = pd.Series(m.sum(axis=0).A1, index=v.get_feature_names_out())
    return s.sort_values().tail(n)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.2, 2.8))
for ax, (rng, name) in zip(axes, [((1, 1), "unigrams: single words"),
                                  ((2, 2), "bigrams: adjacent pairs")]):
    s = ngram_top(rng)
    ax.barh(s.index, s.values, color="#2E6E8E")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10); ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Counting single words splits every phrase. **`topic model`** appears twice in this corpus, but as unigrams it is only `topic` (2) and `model` (5) — and `model` also counts the sentences about language models and machine-learning models, which are a different thing.

```python
CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))      # unigrams AND bigrams
```

Bigrams cost you a much larger, sparser vocabulary, so they are worth it when the phrases carry the meaning — names, technical terms, negations like `not useful`.

# The word-cloud problem {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Why word clouds underperform

A word cloud encodes frequency on **area**, which Cleveland and McGill ranked near the bottom for accuracy, and position on **a packing algorithm**, which carries no meaning at all. A long word also takes more space than a short one at the same frequency.

::: {.gw-box}
**Test:** in a word cloud, can you tell whether the third-most-frequent word beats the fifth? In a sorted bar chart you can read it off. A word cloud can draw someone into a page; it cannot support a comparison, so keep it off the slide where the argument is made.
:::

## The same counts, drawn both ways {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from wordcloud import WordCloud

counts_all = pd.Series(counts.sum(axis=0).A1, index=cv.get_feature_names_out())
wc = WordCloud(width=760, height=430, background_color="white", colormap="Blues",
               prefer_horizontal=0.95, random_state=3
               ).generate_from_frequencies(counts_all.to_dict())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.3))
axes[0].imshow(wc, interpolation="bilinear"); axes[0].axis("off")
axes[0].set_title("Word cloud", fontsize=10)
top10 = counts_all.sort_values().tail(10)
axes[1].barh(top10.index, top10.values, color="#2E6E8E")
axes[1].set_title("Same counts, sorted bars", fontsize=10)
axes[1].tick_params(labelsize=7); axes[1].set_xlabel("occurrences", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same numbers, same 22 documents. **`data` and `text` are tied at 9** — the cloud draws them the same size, but one is dark and one pale, and that colour encodes nothing. **`model` (5) against `chart` (4)** is a 25% difference in count drawn as a 10% difference in height. Finding a given word means scanning the cloud; in the bars it is a lookup.

The cloud still says "this is about data and text" at a glance, which is what a cover image is for. It cannot support a comparison.

## Distinctive vs. frequent: TF–IDF

Raw counts surface what's common *everywhere* ("data"). Often the real question is what makes **this** document different:

$$\text{tf–idf}(t, d) = \underbrace{\text{tf}(t,d)}_{\text{frequent here}} \times \underbrace{\log\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}}_{\text{rare elsewhere}}$$

Same bar chart, different transform. TF–IDF usually answers the more useful question.

## Go back to the sentences: concordance {.smaller}

A bar says `model` appears 5 times. It does not say the word is doing two different jobs.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| classes: plain
def kwic(corpus, term, width=34):
    """Keyword in context: the term with what sits either side of it."""
    rows = []
    for d in corpus:
        toks = d.split()
        for i, w in enumerate(toks):
            if w == term:
                left = " ".join(toks[max(0, i - 6):i])[-width:]
                right = " ".join(toks[i + 1:i + 7])[:width]
                rows.append((f"{left:>{width}}", w, right))
    return rows

for left, w, right in kwic(docs, "model"):
    print(f"{left}  [{w}]  {right}")
```

Five hits, three different senses: a **statistical model** being trained, a **topic model** as a method, and a **language model** as a product. Counting flattens all three into one bar.

::: {.gw-box}
Keyword-in-context is the oldest tool in corpus linguistics and still the fastest check on a frequency chart. Compute the counts, then read a sample of the lines behind the tallest bar before you describe what it means.
:::

# Topics & embeddings {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Topic models: themes from structure

A topic model groups documents by shared vocabulary patterns, with no labels supplied — the same unsupervised idea as Week 6's community detection.

Modern pipeline (**BERTopic**): embed documents → cluster the embeddings → describe each cluster by its distinctive terms. Its built-in visualizations (topic map, term bars, hierarchy) come almost free:

```python
from bertopic import BERTopic
model = BERTopic()
topics, probs = model.fit_transform(docs)
model.visualize_topics()       # interactive topic map
```

*(Static here — BERTopic downloads a language model; you'll run it in Block 2.)*

## Embeddings: text as geometry

An embedding maps each document to a high-dimensional vector where **semantic similarity ≈ proximity**. To see it, we project to 2D — Week 3's PCA instinct again:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import numpy as np
tf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
Xt = tf.fit_transform(docs).toarray()
pcs = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(Xt)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4))
ax.scatter(pcs[:, 0], pcs[:, 1], s=120, color="#2E6E8E")
for i, (x_, y_) in enumerate(pcs):
    ax.annotate(f"doc {i+1}", (x_, y_), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 5), fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("6 documents as TF–IDF vectors, projected to 2D — neighbors share vocabulary")
ax.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC2")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Reading projections honestly {.smaller}

In Block 2 we'll use **UMAP** on real sentence embeddings — far better neighborhoods than this toy PCA. But every projection shares the caveats:

- **Distances are relative**, not metric — "twice as far" means nothing
- Cluster *shapes and sizes* are artifacts of the projection
- Different seeds/parameters → different pictures (Week 6's layout lesson again)

::: {.gw-box}
Name the embedding, the projection and the parameters in the caption. "UMAP of MiniLM embeddings, n_neighbors=15" tells a reader what they are looking at; "semantic map" does not.
:::
